lead: Open large CSV and Excel files in a table you can filter, group and sort. Timeline Explorer is a free program by Eric Zimmerman, made to read the output of forensic parsers.
use_when: A parser such as MFTECmd gave you a CSV with a very large number of rows.
You want to filter by time, user, program or path without writing queries.
You need to read CSV timelines that are too big for a normal spreadsheet.

features.title: Viewing
items: Shows data as a table with one column per field
The project describes it as a viewer for filtering, grouping and sorting

features.title: Working with columns
items: Filter and sort on any column
Group rows by a column to see counts and patterns

features.title: Made for forensic output
items: Used with the CSV output of the other Eric Zimmerman tools
Other guides show it opening KAPE timeline output

requirements: Windows with the .NET 10 Desktop runtime or newer. The current download is for .NET 10 only. The project says to unzip with 7-Zip or WinRAR and not to run it from Program Files unless you run as administrator. It is free, but it is not open source.

steps.title: Install the runtime
steps.text: Install the .NET 10 Desktop runtime from Microsoft if your computer does not have it. Timeline Explorer is a window-based program, so it needs the Desktop runtime.

steps.title: Download and unzip
steps.text: Download TimelineExplorer.zip from Eric Zimmerman's tools page. Unzip it with 7-Zip or WinRAR into a folder such as C:\Tools\TimelineExplorer. Do not use Program Files.

steps.title: Create a CSV to look at
steps.text: Run a parser first, for example MFTECmd with its --csv option. Save the CSV in your case folder. You can also use CSV files produced by KAPE modules.

steps.title: Open the file
steps.text: Start Timeline Explorer and open the CSV. Other guides describe dragging the file onto the window, which also works. Large files can take a short time to load.

steps.title: Sort by time
steps.text: Click a time column header to sort. Look at the period that matters for your case first. Narrowing to the incident window is the usual first move.

steps.title: Filter and group
steps.text: Use the filter on a column to keep only one user, one program or one folder. Use grouping to see which values appear most often. Combine filters step by step and note each one.

steps.title: Save what you need
steps.text: Record the file name, the filters you used and the row numbers of interesting entries in your notes, so another person can reproduce your view.

cases.title: File system timelines
cases.why: MFTECmd output has many rows. Filtering by path or time shows what changed around an incident.

cases.title: Program execution review
cases.why: CSV from Prefetch and Amcache parsers can be filtered on the executable name to follow one program.

cases.title: Single user activity
cases.why: Filtering on a user name column isolates the activity of one account across a large file.

cases.title: Spotting unusual values
cases.why: Grouping by a column shows rare values, such as one odd file path or process among thousands.

cases.title: Triage output from KAPE
cases.why: KAPE modules write CSV files that open directly, so a first look takes only a few minutes.

strengths: Built for the large CSV files that forensic parsers produce.
Sort, filter and group work without any query language.
Fits directly after the command-line tools from the same author.
limits: Free but closed source. The source code is not published.
Windows only, and the current build needs .NET 10.
It is a viewer. It does not parse evidence itself, so you need a parser to make the CSV first.
The project page links no tool-specific manual, so you learn it by trying and from training material.
Very large files need enough memory on your computer.
Filtering is manual. Keep notes of what you applied, or your result is hard to repeat.
